chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, all from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Malik ibn Ayn, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a Christian who died, leaving a son of his Muslim brother and a son of his Muslim sister, and the Christian had children and a Christian wife. children and a Christian wife. He (peace be upon him) said: 'I see that the son of his Muslim brother should be given two-thirds of what he left, and the son of his Muslim sister should be given one-third of what he left, if he does not have young children. But if he has young children, then upon the two inheritors is that they should spend upon the young children from what they inherited from their father, until they mature.'

It was said to him (peace be upon him): 'How should they spend?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The inheritor of the two-thirds should take out two-thirds of the expenses, and the inheritor of the one-third should take out one-third of the expenses. And if they mature, they cease the expenses for them.'

It was said to him (peace be upon him): 'And if the children become Muslim while they are young?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever their father left should be handed over to the Imam (peace be upon him) until they mature. If they remain upon Islam, the Imam hands over their inheritance to them. And if they do not remain upon Islam when they mature, the Imam hands over their inheritance to the son of his brother and the son of his sister, the two Muslims. He hands over to the son of the brother two-thirds of what was left, and he hands over to the son of the sister one-third of what was left.'
ai.seo_question: What are the inheritance rules for a Christian leaving Muslim cousins and non-Muslim minor children?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the specific inheritance distribution for a Christian decedent, prioritizing Muslim agnatic cousins (son of brother and son of sister) over non-Muslim offspring, reflecting the Shia principle of 'al-muslim yurath wa la al-kafir' (the Muslim inherits, but the non-Muslim does not). It further establishes a practical mechanism where the Muslim heirs bear the financial responsibility for the minors' maintenance, ensuring their upbringing is supported from the estate itself. The ruling also accounts for the theological status of the minors, stipulating that if they convert to Islam before maturity, their share is held in trust by the Imam until they reach adulthood, safeguarding their potential claim to the inheritance.
